title: Road to Candidate Master
tagline: A Codeforces-only ladder that turns the Module 1 algorithm toolbox into rating. Every problem is real, curated by popularity, and grouped by the pattern it trains.

phases.title: Foundations
phases.summary: Get fast and accurate at the basics. The whole game here is reading carefully, coding cleanly, and not failing on edge cases. Aim to solve A/B of most Div.2 rounds on autopilot.

themes.title: Implementation & Simulation
themes.blurb: Most Div.2 A/B problems are just 'do exactly what the statement says, without bugs'. Speed and correctness here free up your clock for the harder problems later in the round.
signals: The statement describes a concrete process step by step.
Small constraints (n ≤ 2·10^5, often much smaller) and no obvious 'trick'.
You can already see the answer — the only risk is an off-by-one or an edge case.
themes.technique: Translate the statement into code literally, then hunt edge cases: empty input, n = 1, all-equal elements, max values (watch overflow → use 64-bit).
themes.trap: Rushing and missing a corner case. Re-read the constraints and the output format before submitting; a single wrong-answer on pretest 2 costs more time than a careful read.
themes.goal: Solve these in under 10 minutes each with zero penalty.

themes.title: Math & Parity Basics
themes.blurb: A huge fraction of easy problems collapse to one observation: parity, divisibility, a closed-form sum, or a gcd. Train yourself to look for the formula first.
signals: Answer asked for huge n — you can't simulate, you must find a formula.
Words like 'even/odd', 'divisible', 'multiple of', 'sum of first k'.
Tiny output (a single number) from large input.
themes.technique: Compute small cases by hand, spot the pattern, prove it with parity/divisibility/arithmetic-series reasoning. Keep gcd, lcm and n(n+1)/2 in muscle memory.
themes.trap: Integer overflow on the closed form — sums of n up to 1e9 overflow 32-bit. Use 64-bit everywhere.
themes.goal: See the formula within 2–3 small examples instead of coding a loop.

problems.name: Arpa’s hard exam and Mehrdad’s naive cheat

themes.title: First Greedy Moves
themes.blurb: Sort, then take the best available choice. Easy greedies are about *ordering* the input the right way and proving the obvious move is safe.
signals: 'Maximize / minimize' with no dependency between choices.
Sorting the input makes the decision obvious.
Each step has a clearly 'best' local option.
themes.technique: Sort by the right key, then sweep. Ask 'why is taking the best item now never wrong?' — that's your exchange argument.
themes.trap: Greedy that *feels* right but isn't. If you can't argue why a local choice is globally safe, suspect DP.
themes.goal: Recognise the sort key instantly.

themes.title: Brute Force & Search Spaces
themes.blurb: When n is tiny, just try everything. The skill is recognising that the search space is small enough (2^n, n!, or n^2/n^3) to enumerate.
signals: n ≤ 20 → subsets (2^n).  n ≤ 10 → permutations (n!).
Constraints far smaller than usual — the setter is inviting brute force.
'Choose some subset / arrangement that...'
themes.technique: Estimate the work: 2^n, n!, or nested loops. If it fits ~10^8, enumerate and check each candidate.
themes.trap: Misjudging the size — 2^25 is 3·10^7 (fine), 2^40 is not. Always do the back-of-envelope count first.
themes.goal: Map constraints → enumeration size in seconds.

themes.title: Two Pointers & Sorting Tricks
themes.blurb: After sorting, a pair of indices sweeping the array answers a surprising number of 'find a pair / a window' questions in linear time.
signals: 'Find two elements with sum / difference X' on a sortable array.
'Longest / shortest contiguous segment such that ...'.
Monotonic relationship: moving one pointer only ever moves the other one way.
themes.technique: Sort if order doesn't matter, then advance L/R based on whether the current window is too big or too small.
themes.trap: Using two pointers when the window condition isn't monotonic — then you need a different tool.
themes.goal: Reach for sort + two pointers reflexively on pair/window prompts.

phases.title: Climbing to Specialist
phases.summary: Now C-level problems need a real idea. This phase is where binary search, prefix sums, constructive thinking and basic graph/DP first appear. Pattern recognition starts paying off hard here.

themes.title: Binary Search
themes.blurb: Binary search on a sorted array — and, more powerfully, on the *answer*. If a boolean check is monotonic, you can binary search the smallest/largest value that passes.
signals: 'Minimum / maximum value such that some condition holds.'
A check(x) that is monotonic: false…false,true…true.
Sorted data + 'how many ≤ x' style queries.
themes.technique: Define check(x) carefully, prove monotonicity, then standard lo/hi loop. Decide [lo,hi) vs [lo,hi] and stick to it.
themes.trap: Off-by-one in the boundary and an infinite loop when lo/hi don't converge. Write the invariant down.
themes.goal: Spot 'binary search the answer' from the phrase 'minimum maximum'.

themes.title: Constructive Algorithms
themes.blurb: Codeforces' signature genre: 'construct ANY valid object'. There's no search — you invent a pattern that always works and prove it does.
signals: 'Construct any array/permutation/grid such that ...'.
Often 'print -1 if impossible' — first nail the impossibility condition.
Small examples in the statement that hint at a repeating structure.
themes.technique: Play with n=1,2,3 by hand, find a repeatable pattern (alternate, pair up, snake, halve), then argue it always satisfies the constraints.
themes.trap: Forgetting the -1 case, or a construction that breaks on the smallest n. Always test n=1 and n=2.
themes.goal: Build intuition for 'invent a pattern' problems — these are free rating once it clicks.

themes.title: Number Theory Basics
themes.blurb: Primes, divisors, gcd and modular arithmetic. The sieve and divisor enumeration in √n unlock most early number-theory problems.
signals: 'Count divisors / primes', 'is it prime', 'gcd of subarray'.
Numbers up to 10^6 → precompute a sieve / smallest prime factor.
Anything 'modulo 10^9+7'.
themes.technique: Sieve for primality/factorisation up to 1e6; trial-divide to √n for a single number; use gcd identities for subarray-gcd tricks.
themes.trap: O(n) divisor loops when √n suffices; forgetting that gcd of a range only ever decreases.
themes.goal: Know instantly whether to sieve or trial-divide.

problems.name: Omkar and Last Class of Math

themes.title: Greedy + Sorting
themes.blurb: The workhorse combo: sort by a clever key, then make the locally optimal choice. The hard part is choosing the key and proving the exchange argument.
signals: Pairing / scheduling / assigning to minimise or maximise a total.
Two arrays you can reorder independently.
'If I swap two adjacent choices, the answer doesn't improve.'
themes.technique: Guess a sort key, then prove with an exchange argument: any optimal solution can be reordered to match the greedy without getting worse.
themes.trap: Sorting by the wrong attribute (e.g. by deadline vs by length). Test the greedy against brute force on tiny inputs.
themes.goal: Derive and trust the exchange argument under contest pressure.

problems.name: Anna and the Valentine's Day Gift

themes.title: Graph Traversal (BFS / DFS)
themes.blurb: Connected components, flood fill, shortest path in an unweighted graph, cycle detection. BFS/DFS is the backbone of half of CP.
signals: Grid or explicit graph; 'connected regions', 'reachable', 'components'.
Unweighted shortest path → plain BFS.
'Is there a cycle', 'is it bipartite', 'color the graph'.
themes.technique: Model the state as nodes/edges, pick BFS (layers / shortest steps) or DFS (connectivity / recursion), and track a visited set.
themes.trap: Recursion-depth stack overflow on big graphs (use an explicit stack / iterative DFS); revisiting nodes without a visited check.
themes.goal: Translate a word problem into a graph automatically.

problems.name: Mahmoud and Ehab and the bipartiteness

themes.title: Intro Dynamic Programming
themes.blurb: 1-D DP: count ways, min cost, can-you-reach. The leap is seeing the problem as a sequence of decisions with overlapping subproblems.
signals: 'Number of ways', 'minimum cost', 'can you reach' with sequential choices.
Exponential brute force that obviously repeats subproblems.
Choice at step i depends only on a few earlier states.
themes.technique: Define dp[i] in words first ('best answer using first i'), write the transition, set the base case, decide iteration order.
themes.trap: Wrong base case / iteration order, or a state that doesn't capture enough information. State design is 80% of DP.
themes.goal: Phrase a clean dp[i] definition before touching code.

problems.name: Given Length and Sum of Digits...

phases.title: Becoming Expert
phases.summary: The Expert wall. Problems now combine two ideas: binary-search-on-answer with a greedy check, DP with bitmasks, graphs with DSU. This is where deliberate pattern practice separates Experts from stuck Specialists.

themes.title: Binary Search on the Answer
themes.blurb: The classic Expert combo: binary search the answer, and the feasibility check is itself a greedy or simulation. Recognising the monotonic check is the whole skill.
signals: 'Maximise the minimum' or 'minimise the maximum'.
Splitting / allocating with a threshold that gets easier as the threshold relaxes.
A check(x) you can verify greedily in O(n).
themes.technique: Binary search x; write a greedy check(x). Prove that if x works, so does every easier x (monotonicity).
themes.trap: A check that isn't actually monotonic, or an O(n log n) check that makes the whole thing too slow.
themes.goal: Decompose into 'search the value' + 'greedy verify'.

themes.title: Classic DP Patterns
themes.blurb: Knapsack, LIS, LCS, partition, grid DP — the named patterns. Most mid-level DP is one of these wearing a costume.
signals: Subset-sum / 'pick items under a budget' → knapsack.
'Longest increasing / common subsequence' → LIS / LCS.
2-D grid with moves → grid DP.
themes.technique: Match to the closest named pattern, then adapt the state. Remember LIS in O(n log n) via patience sorting / lower_bound.
themes.trap: Memory blowup on 2-D DP — roll the array to one row when only the previous row is needed.
themes.goal: Instantly classify which classic pattern fits.

themes.title: Disjoint Set Union (DSU)
themes.blurb: Union-Find answers 'are these connected?' under merges, near-instantly. It also powers Kruskal's MST and offline connectivity tricks.
signals: Edges added over time; 'are u and v connected now?'.
Counting / sizing connected components after unions.
Kruskal MST, or grouping elements by an equivalence relation.
themes.technique: Path compression + union by size/rank → near-O(1). For 'connectivity over deletions', process queries offline in reverse.
themes.trap: Forgetting to union by size/rank (degrades to O(n)); using find without path compression.
themes.goal: See merges-over-time → DSU automatically.

themes.title: Weighted Shortest Paths
themes.blurb: Dijkstra (non-negative), Bellman-Ford (negative edges / k steps), Floyd-Warshall (all pairs, small n). Pick by the edge weights and graph size.
signals: Weighted edges + 'shortest / cheapest path'.
Non-negative weights → Dijkstra; negative or 'at most k edges' → Bellman-Ford.
n ≤ 500 and all-pairs distances → Floyd-Warshall.
themes.technique: Dijkstra with a heap and stale-entry skipping; sometimes the state is (node, extra) — a layered graph. Floyd-Warshall for transitive-closure style problems.
themes.trap: Running Dijkstra with negative edges; 32-bit overflow on summed weights.
themes.goal: Choose the right shortest-path algorithm from weights + n.

problems.name: Lunar New Year and a Wander

themes.title: Modular Arithmetic & Number Theory
themes.blurb: Fast exponentiation, modular inverses, factorisation by smallest-prime, and counting with divisors. The mod 10^9+7 toolkit.
signals: 'Compute X mod p' for huge X, or a^b mod p.
Division under a modulus → modular inverse (Fermat).
Counting multiples / coprimes / divisor sums.
themes.technique: Binary exponentiation for powers and inverses; precompute smallest-prime-factor for fast factorisation; inclusion–exclusion over prime factors.
themes.trap: Negative values mod p (normalise with ((x%p)+p)%p); inverse of a non-coprime number.
themes.goal: Fluent modular algebra under contest time.

themes.title: String Matching & Hashing
themes.blurb: Prefix-functions (KMP), Z-array, and polynomial hashing turn substring questions into O(n). Hashing is the universal 'are these equal?' hammer.
signals: 'Does pattern occur', 'count occurrences', 'longest border/period'.
Compare many substrings for equality → polynomial hashing.
Prefix = suffix structure → KMP failure function / Z.
themes.technique: KMP/Z for occurrences and periods; double hashing (two mods) to kill collisions; precompute prefix hashes for O(1) substring compares.
themes.trap: Single-mod hash collisions on adversarial tests; mismatched base/mod between strings.
themes.goal: Reduce substring questions to hashing or a prefix function.

themes.title: Bit Tricks & Bitmask Enumeration
themes.blurb: Treat a set / small array as the bits of an integer. XOR/AND/OR identities and subset enumeration solve a whole class of 'choose a subset' problems.
signals: n ≤ 20–22 and 'choose a subset / partition'.
XOR-based conditions, 'pair up so that ...'.
Bitwise AND/OR/XOR of a range or subset.
themes.technique: Iterate masks 0..2^n-1; enumerate submasks with the (m-1)&mask trick; reason bit-by-bit for AND/OR/XOR constraints (each bit independent).
themes.trap: Confusing submask vs supermask iteration; forgetting bit independence simplifies the problem.
themes.goal: Map 'small set' problems to integer bitmasks.

themes.title: Sliding Window & Prefix Sums
themes.blurb: A window that grows/shrinks to maintain an invariant, backed by prefix sums for O(1) range queries. The linear-time answer to many 'segment' problems.
signals: 'Longest / number of subarrays with property P' where P is monotonic in length.
Range-sum queries → prefix sums (or prefix XOR / counts).
Count pairs (i,j) with a sum/condition via a running map.
themes.technique: Expand right, shrink left while the window violates P; precompute prefix arrays so any range is O(1).
themes.trap: Non-monotonic conditions break the window; prefix-sum overflow.
themes.goal: Default to window + prefix sums on subarray prompts.

themes.title: Counting & Combinatorics
themes.blurb: Count arrangements with nCr, the stars-and-bars trick, and inclusion–exclusion — all under a modulus with precomputed factorials.
signals: 'How many ways / arrangements / sequences', answer mod p.
Distribute identical items → stars and bars.
'At least one' / 'none of' constraints → inclusion–exclusion.
themes.technique: Precompute factorials + inverse factorials for O(1) nCr mod p; decompose the count into independent choices; subtract bad cases with inclusion–exclusion.
themes.trap: Forgetting modular inverse for division; double counting symmetric arrangements.
themes.goal: Break a count into independent multiplicative choices.

phases.title: The Candidate Master Push
phases.summary: The target tier. Data structures (segment trees / Fenwick), tree DP, advanced DP states, and SCC-level graph theory. Problems reward a deep toolbox plus the judgement to combine tools. This is the heart of the roadmap.

themes.title: Segment Trees & Fenwick
themes.blurb: Point-update / range-query in O(log n). Fenwick for sums and inversion counting; segment trees for min/max/gcd and more. The CM-level data-structure backbone.
signals: Many range queries + point updates interleaved.
Count inversions / 'elements smaller to the right' → Fenwick.
Range min/max/sum/gcd with updates → segment tree.
themes.technique: Fenwick for prefix-aggregate + point update; segment tree for any associative range op; coordinate-compress when values are large.
themes.trap: Off-by-one in 1-indexed Fenwick; forgetting to compress coordinates.
themes.goal: Reach for a BIT/segtree the moment you see range query + update.

themes.title: Tree Algorithms & LCA
themes.blurb: Rooting, subtree sizes, diameter, LCA, and distance queries. The standard tree toolkit that shows up in nearly every CM round.
signals: Input is a tree (n nodes, n-1 edges).
'Distance between u and v', 'kth ancestor' → LCA (binary lifting).
'Longest path' → diameter via two BFS / DFS.
themes.technique: Root the tree, compute subtree sizes / depths with one DFS; binary-lifting LCA for distance and ancestor queries.
themes.trap: Recursion depth on a path-shaped tree (10^5 deep) → iterative DFS or raise the limit.
themes.goal: Apply the rooted-tree toolkit on sight.

themes.title: DP on Trees
themes.blurb: Combine children's answers into the parent's. Add rerooting to get the answer for every node in O(n). A signature CM skill.
signals: Tree + 'best/count over subtrees' or 'for every root'.
Answer at a node depends on its children's answers.
'Maximum independent set / matching / path' on a tree.
themes.technique: Post-order DFS to fold children up; for 'answer for all roots', do a second DFS passing the parent's contribution down (rerooting).
themes.trap: Mixing up which child contributions to exclude during rerooting; deep recursion.
themes.goal: Design subtree states and reroot confidently.

problems.name: A and B and Lecture Rooms

themes.title: Advanced DP States
themes.blurb: Bitmask DP over subsets, interval DP, and digit DP. The state stops being a single index and becomes a richer object — the key creative leap to CM.
signals: n ≤ 20 with 'visit all / assign all' → bitmask DP (TSP-like).
'Combine adjacent segments optimally' → interval DP.
'Count numbers ≤ N with a digit property' → digit DP.
themes.technique: Bitmask DP: dp[mask] over visited sets. Interval DP: dp[l][r] over a split point. Digit DP: dp[pos][tight][state] over the decimal expansion.
themes.trap: 2^n · n blowing the time budget; forgetting the 'tight' flag in digit DP.
themes.goal: Recognise which non-trivial DP state the problem needs.

themes.title: SCC, Topo & Graph Structure
themes.blurb: Condense a directed graph into its strongly-connected components, then work on the resulting DAG. Topological order powers DAG DP and dependency problems.
signals: Directed graph with cycles you want to collapse.
'Group mutually reachable nodes', 'minimum to make strongly connected'.
DAG + longest/critical path → topo-order DP.
themes.technique: Tarjan / Kosaraju for SCC → condensation DAG; topological sort then DP along the order. Implication graphs (2-SAT flavour) reduce to SCC.
themes.trap: Treating the original graph as a DAG before condensing; cycle handling in topo sort.
themes.goal: Condense to a DAG, then solve on the DAG.

themes.title: Hard Constructive & Greedy
themes.blurb: CM-level constructive: the pattern is subtle and the proof matters. These build the 'invent + justify' muscle that defines a strong Expert/CM.
signals: 'Construct such that ...' with a non-obvious global constraint.
Interactive or adaptive flavour, or a tight bound on operations.
A clean answer once you spot the right invariant.
themes.technique: Find an invariant the construction must preserve; build greedily while maintaining it; prove optimality / validity by that invariant.
themes.trap: A construction that passes small cases but violates the bound at scale. Stress-test against brute force.
themes.goal: Invent and *prove* constructions under pressure.

themes.title: Harder Math & Probability
themes.blurb: Expected value, probability, and combinatorial identities — usually mod p. Linearity of expectation turns scary problems into a sum of easy ones.
signals: 'Expected value of ...', 'probability that ...'.
A sum over all pairs / subsets that you can swap order on.
Counting with symmetry → Burnside-lite reasoning.
themes.technique: Linearity of expectation: sum each element's contribution independently; swap summation order; combinatorial identities to collapse sums.
themes.trap: Treating dependent events as independent; modular inverse of probabilities.
themes.goal: Reach for linearity of expectation reflexively.

phases.title: Toward Master
phases.summary: Beyond CM. Lazy segment trees, DP optimisation, suffix structures, matrix exponentiation, and divide & conquer. Fewer new tools — deeper combinations and sharper proofs. Solve these and CM is comfortably behind you.

themes.title: Lazy Segment Trees
themes.blurb: Range-update + range-query with lazy propagation, segment-tree-on-DP, and beats-style tricks. The heavy data-structure end of CM→Master.
signals: Range assign/add + range aggregate queries.
DP transitions that are really range updates over an index.
'Apply an operation to a whole segment' repeatedly.
themes.technique: Push lazy tags down before recursing; compose tags carefully. Recognise when a DP recurrence is a segment-tree range operation in disguise.
themes.trap: Tag composition order bugs; forgetting to push down before a query.
themes.goal: Wield lazy propagation and segtree-accelerated DP.

themes.title: DP Optimisation & Divide-and-Conquer
themes.blurb: Speeding up O(n^2) DP: divide-and-conquer optimisation, convex-hull trick, and Knuth. Plus D&C as an algorithmic technique in its own right.
signals: An O(n^2) DP that's too slow and has a monotone optimal split point.
Transitions of the form dp[i] = min(dp[j] + cost(j,i)).
Cost satisfies the quadrangle inequality → Knuth / D&C opt.
themes.technique: Prove monotonicity of the optimal split, then divide-and-conquer over it; or maintain lines for the convex-hull trick.
themes.trap: Applying an optimisation without verifying its monotonicity/convexity precondition.
themes.goal: Spot when an O(n^2) DP can drop to O(n log n).

problems.name: Max to the Right of Min

themes.title: Suffix Structures & Heavy Strings
themes.blurb: Suffix arrays / automata, plus hashing combined with data structures. The high end of string problems where naive matching is far too slow.
signals: 'Number of distinct substrings', 'longest repeated/common substring'.
Many substring comparisons across queries.
Lexicographic ordering of all suffixes.
themes.technique: Suffix array + LCP for distinct-substring and ordering questions; suffix automaton for substring counting; hashing + a data structure for ad-hoc queries.
themes.trap: Hash collisions at scale; the constant factor of suffix structures timing out.
themes.goal: Choose the right suffix structure for the query type.

themes.title: Matrix Exponentiation
themes.blurb: When a linear recurrence must be evaluated at huge n, raise its transition matrix to the n-th power in O(k^3 log n). Counts paths of length n, too.
signals: Linear recurrence evaluated at n up to 10^18.
'Number of walks of length n' in a small graph.
A state vector updated by the same linear map every step.
themes.technique: Write the transition as a matrix, then binary-exponentiate it under the modulus. Adjacency-matrix power counts fixed-length walks.
themes.trap: Cubic multiply too slow if k is large; modular overflow in the matrix product.
themes.goal: Recognise 'linear recurrence at huge n' → matrix power.

themes.title: Divide & Conquer
themes.blurb: Split, solve, and merge — counting cross-boundary contributions in the merge step. Inversions, closest pair, and CDQ-style offline tricks.
signals: Count pairs (i<j) with some relation → count across the split in merge.
A problem that halves cleanly with a cheap combine.
Offline queries sortable into a divide-and-conquer over time.
themes.technique: Recurse on halves, then count/merge cross-pairs in O(n) (as in merge-sort inversion counting); CDQ for 3-D dominance offline.
themes.trap: An expensive merge step that breaks the O(n log n); double-counting cross pairs.
themes.goal: Identify the cheap cross-boundary merge.

problems.name: I've Been Flipping Numbers for 300 Years and Calculated the Sum

themes.title: Advanced Counting
themes.blurb: Counting that fuses combinatorics with DP: count configurations, count with forbidden patterns, count over structures. The proof-heavy Master end.
signals: 'Count the number of valid X' where X has rich structure.
DP whose value is itself a count, combined with binomials.
Inclusion–exclusion layered over a DP.
themes.technique: Set up a counting DP, fold in nCr factors, and subtract invalid configurations via inclusion–exclusion. Keep everything mod p.
themes.trap: Off-by-one in inclusion–exclusion signs; overcounting symmetric structures.
themes.goal: Fuse combinatorial identities with DP states.
